title: Quantum Reservoir Computing: Recent Advances and Future Directions
authors: Shehbaz Tariq, Muhammad Talha, Arshid Ali, Muhammad Diyan, Symeon Chatzinotas
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses the dynamics of a fixed or weakly tuned quantum system to transform temporal and sequential inputs into measured features, while training is typically confined to a classical readout. This separation reduces reliance on repeated quantum parameter updates and avoids the barren plateaus associated with variational circuit training. Its computational power is often attributed to the exponentially large Hilbert space of the quantum system. However, the memory, nonlinearity, and expressivity that determine what a reservoir can actually compute depend jointly on the input encoding, quantum evolution, observables, measurement, and readout, not on Hilbert space dimension alone. On hardware, these capabilities are further constrained by finite sampling, hardware noise, measurement backaction, and the cost of estimating observables, so a large state space alone does not guarantee useful computation. In this survey, we develop a common system model that connects these components and use it to organize QRC foundations, computational properties, reservoir architectures, operating protocols, and physical implementations. We examine spin, photonic, superconducting, bosonic, neutral atom, and other analog platforms, together with applications, software and high performance computing support, benchmarking, and reproducibility. The analysis distinguishes hardware demonstrations from simulations and identifies the assumptions and resources that govern comparisons across implementations. Current results do not establish a broad quantum advantage over well matched classical reservoirs. We therefore specify the resource accounting, benchmark standards, and theoretical criteria needed to evaluate claims of quantum advantage.
summary: This survey establishes a unified system model for Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC), detailing the necessary components from input encoding to classical readout across diverse hardware platforms. It critically analyzes that computational power depends on the entire processing chain, not just Hilbert space size. The work aims to define rigorous benchmarking standards needed to substantiate claims of quantum advantage in this emerging field.
main_problem: Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) aims to leverage quantum dynamics for feature extraction from time-series data in machine learning, while overcoming limitations related to hardware constraints and establishing clear benchmarks.
main_result: The paper develops a comprehensive system model connecting all components of QRC—from input encoding through reservoir evolution to classical readout—and provides a framework for evaluating true quantum advantage.
method: It proposes a hybrid computational approach where the quantum processor (QPU) handles the non-linear dynamics, and classical high-performance computing (HPC) manages preprocessing, optimization, and final readout.
model_or_system: The system is modeled through distinct stages: input encoding ($ho_{t,0} = E(\dots)$), reservoir evolution ($ho_{t,v} = R(\dots)$), measurement ($z_t$), and classical readout. Platforms examined include spin, photonic, superconducting, bosonic, and neutral atom systems.
key_observables: Feature vector $z_t$ (from measurement) and prediction $b_{yt}$ (from readout); memory, nonlinearity, and expressivity are key diagnostic properties.
important_parameters: Fixed or selected parameters ($\lambda_p, \lambda_e, \lambda_H$) governing preprocessing, encoding, and dynamics; finite sampling rates and hardware noise levels are critical constraints.
main_assumptions: The computational power depends jointly on the input encoding, quantum evolution, observables, measurement, and readout, not just Hilbert space dimension. Current results do not guarantee a broad quantum advantage over classical methods.
figures_summary: Figure 1 outlines the survey's organization across foundations to benchmarking; Figure 2 illustrates the integrated QRC stack connecting classical preprocessing, reservoir dynamics, measurement, and classical readout.
paper_structure: The paper organizes QRC by developing a common system model that connects all processing stages. It then surveys computational properties, discusses various reservoir architectures (spin, photonic, etc.), outlines operating protocols, and addresses benchmarking standards to evaluate quantum advantage claims.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for analyzing how physical implementations of quantum dynamics can be mapped onto machine learning tasks, which is highly relevant for understanding resource requirements in open quantum systems modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Organization and analytical flow of the survey.

Figure 2: Integrated QRC stack. Classical preprocessing maps application data to inputs accepted by the quantum interface. Reservoir evolution generates a state trajectory, measurement converts selected properties of that trajectory into classical features, and the readout maps those features to predictions. Finite sampling and measurement disturbance depend on the operating protocol. The surrounding blocks show representative hardware, software, execution resources, and task domains.

Figure 3: Timeline of representative QRC experiments, models, and related physical reservoir studies from 2018 to 2026. Color denotes the platform family and marker style denotes the study type. Bubble text reports the physical scale or measured resource stated in each study. These quantities are heterogeneous and are not directly comparable as reservoir capacity. The entries cover spin, NMR, and magnonic systems [56, 96, 98]; photonic, CV, bosonic, and quantum dot systems [1, 29, 102, 129]; superconducting, microwave, and circuit QED systems [23, 55, 116, 144]; and a neutral atom implementation [69].
